# Understanding the superconductivity and charge density wave interaction through quasi-static lattice fluctuations

**Authors:** Zach Porter; Lingjia Shen; Rajan Plumley; Nicolas G Burdet; Alexander N Petsch; Jiajia Wen; Nathan C Drucker; Cheng Peng; Xiaoqian M Chen; Andrei Fluerasu; Elizabeth Blackburn; Giacomo Coslovich; David G Hawthorn; Joshua J Turner

Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138 | fDepartment of Condensed Matter Physics and Materials Science, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY 11973 | gDivision of Synchrotron Radiation Research, Lund University, Lund SE-22100, Sweden | hDepartment of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON N2L 3G1, Canada

## Abstract

In high-Tc cuprate superconductors, coupling between electrons and the crystal lattice yields complex phases of matter. Phases such as the charge density wave (CDW) state can intertwine with superconductivity, but it is not known how. We show that coherent X-rays can be used to measure slow, subtle fluctuations of the atomic lattice in YBa2Cu3O6+y, giving information on these phases. Surprisingly, we measure the response of these fluctuations to both superconductivity and CDW. These results add to our fundamental understanding of how superconductivity, CDW, and the lattice are coupled on quasi-static timescales.

Keywords: superconductivity, fluctuations, X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, cuprates

## Abstract

In unconventional superconductors, coupled charge and lattice degrees of freedom can manifest in ordered phases of matter that are intertwined. In the cuprate family, fluctuating short-range charge correlations can coalesce into a longer-range charge density wave (CDW) order which is thought to intertwine with superconductivity, yet the nature of the interaction is still poorly understood. Here, by measuring subtle lattice fluctuations in underdoped YBa2Cu3O6+y on quasi-static timescales (thousands of seconds) through X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, we report sensitivity to both superconductivity and CDW. The atomic lattice shows remarkably faster relaxational dynamics upon approaching the superconducting transition at Tc ≈ 65 K. By tracking the momentum dependence, we show that the intermediate scattering function almost monotonically scales with the relaxation distance of atoms away from their average positions above Tc and in the presence of the CDW state, while this peculiar trend is reversed for other temperatures. These observations are consistent with an incipient CDW stabilized by local strain. This work provides insights into the crucial role of relaxational atomic fluctuations for understanding the electronic physics cuprates, which are inherently disordered due to carrier doping.

The interactions between charge and lattice degrees of freedom in unconventional superconductors comprise a fascinating research direction in condensed matter physics (1, 2). Critical to this discussion is the dynamical behavior between broken symmetry states with similar energy scales, and how different fluctuations relate to the superconducting state. Charge density wave (CDW) correlations in hole-doped cuprates result from interdependent electronic degrees of freedom, and result in nanoscale “puddles” of phase separation with glassy charge fluctuations (3–8). CDW order has been observed in cuprates for almost three decades and has been studied using a variety of techniques—from scanning tunneling microscopy to NMR to X-ray scattering (9–12). While much is known about the static, average CDW structure and its response to different excitation mechanisms (13–18), its driving mechanism and how it intertwines with the superconductivity are still debated.

Here, we address these open questions by studying the CDW and superconducting states through measurement of spontaneous atomic lattice relaxation in underdoped YBa2Cu3O6+y (y = 0.67, YBCO). By illuminating a heterogeneous sample with coherent X-rays, interference from objects compatible with the wavelength (here about 1 Å) produces speckle with a coherence area set by the transverse coherence length of the source. A speckle pattern thus acts as a fingerprint of the spatial arrangements of the domains (19, 20). By tracking the evolution of the speckle pattern in the diffuse scattering near a lattice Bragg peak, one can study the temporal dynamics of atomic relaxation caused by local strain. In the cuprates, relaxational atomic fluctuations can respond to the CDWs, because the diffuse scattering underlying the X-ray speckle is driven by CDW-related atomic distortions (21). In YBa2Cu3O6+y, we identify an especially fast response near the superconducting transition Tc, and report on the momentum dependence of atomic relaxation, which supports an incipient CDW state stabilized by local strain. This work reveals that measuring lattice fluctuations with bright, coherent X-ray beams can provide spatially resolved details about the correlation physics in complex materials.

A representative measurement in Fig. 1A shows the diffuse X-ray scattering near the Bragg reflection q = (0, 0, 5). This reflection was chosen for two reasons. First of all, a specular reflection has minimal unwanted diffuse scattering contributions from any residual local orthorhombic twinning in the ab plane, although our sample has been globally detwinned. Moreover, it has the highest structure factor among the accessible specular reflections, hence possessing the strongest diffuse scattering signal based on continuum elastic theory (22). The sharp streaky feature close to the vertical direction arises from crystal truncation rod (CTR) because our scattering plane is vertical. In Fig. 1A, there are also irregular scattering features in the horizontal direction. Since they only show up at a few temperatures, we ascribe them to surface defects.

*Fig. 1.: XPCS shows anomalous dynamics near the superconducting transition Tc. (A) Average diffraction pattern for time-domain measurements collected at 60 K for 5,400 s at a frame rate of 1 Hz. The four gray annuli together define the region of interest. The horizontal (vertical) direction is approximately in-plane (out-of-plane), as denoted by q | | ( q ⊥ ). (B) Comparison of | F ( Δ q , t ) | 2 at several temperatures within one region of interest; binned data are symbols and fits are lines described in the text. Note how the captured dynamics are nonmonotonic in temperature.*

We define the relative momentum transfer Δ q via a polar coordinate system centered at this q in the detector plane. One ring-shaped region of interest with fixed radius Δ q is shown in Fig. 1A. It has four annuli because pixel regions contaminated by the CTR and irregular scattering need to be masked. To ensure consistency in analysis, the same mask treatment has been applied to all temperatures. We track the speckle correlation in time using conventional X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) analysis. In Fig. 1B, we show the absolute squared modulus of the intermediate scattering function | F ( Δ q , t ) | 2 . This can be calculated from the intensity–intensity autocorrelation function g 2 ( q , t ) via the Siegert relation | F ( q , t ) | 2 = [ g 2 ( q , t ) − 1 ] / β 0 , where β0 is the XPCS contrast factor and t is the time delay (23–25). Details of this calculation and subsequent analysis are in SI Appendix. The dynamics of the system are captured by | F ( q , t ) | 2 : A value of 1 indicates the system is fully correlated (static) at a delay time t when compared with its initial state, whereas a value of 0 indicates full decorrelation. The time required for decorrelation in XPCS ( | F ( q , t ) | 2 → 0 ) therefore encodes the fluctuating timescale for the scatterers. Applying this knowledge to Fig. 1B, we see that the relaxational atomic fluctuations in YBCO are on the timescale of 103 s, and more intriguingly, show a strong and remarkably nonmonotonic temperature dependence.

To quantify the timescale evolution for each of the measured temperatures, we numerically examine the intermediate scattering function | F ( q , t ) | 2 . Fits to this function are shown as solid lines in Fig. 1B. It is evident that two distinct time constants are present, we therefore fit the data to a double stretched exponential form (26):

$$ [1] | F ( q , t ) | 2 = ( a e − ( t / τ 1 ) β + ( 1 − a ) e − ( t / τ 2 ) β ) 2 $$

to extract the relaxation lifetimes τ1 and τ2, shown in Fig. 2. τ1 is the major relaxation channel with fraction a centered around 80% (SI Appendix, Fig. S2D) below T CDW ≈ 150 K, the onset temperature of CDWs in YBa2Cu3O6+y at zero magnetic field (27). At 15 K, 45 K, and above T CDW , the τ2 channel cannot be unambiguously determined. Eq. 1 thus reduces to the τ1 term. The stretching exponent β is found to be centered around 1.35 (SI Appendix, Fig. S2B). As a result, we fix it to this value, which reflects the cooperative “cascadic” dynamics expected for charge-ordered condensed matter systems (26, 28), for all temperatures in the final fit. Both time constants τ 1 , 2 increase as temperature decreases from T CDW to Tc. And both time constants show an anomaly at the superconducting critical temperature Tc, the origin of which we discuss further below.

*Fig. 2.: Anomalous dynamics in the XPCS temperature dependence. Fitted exponential time constants τ1 (main panel) and τ2 (shown in main panel for comparison and enlarged in Inset) as a function of temperature at one value of Δ q = 19 × 10 − 3 Å−1 (Eq. 1). Solid blue lines are a guide to the eye, and error bar calculations are described in Materials and Methods. Overplotted in the main panel is the CDW peak amplitude (gray line) measured on the same sample (27), which is a static measurement of the charge order. For T = 15 K, T = 45 K, and above 150 K, the fraction of the τ2 term is negligibly small, so it is not shown.*

In Fig. 2, clearly the static CDW amplitude response at Tc (gray solid line) is less drastic than the corresponding lattice relaxational response (blue symbols). It is also notable that both time constants show an anomaly at the critical temperature Tc, and differ by about an order of magnitude. In order to understand the two relaxation channels in | F ( q , t ) | 2 , we turn to evaluate | F ( q , t ) | 2 as a function of Δ q . The results are summarized in Fig. 3.

*Fig. 3.: Momentum-dependent changes associated with charge order. (A) | F ( Δ q , t ) | 2 at two representative temperatures with regions of interest at several momentum transfers Δ q . The time constant decreases with increasing momentum transfer for T = 65 K (Left, downward triangles), yet the opposite dependence is observed for T = 115 K (Right, upward triangles). (B) The momentum dependence for normalized | F ( Δ q , t ) | 2 at fixed time delay t = 1 , 000 s, shown for several temperatures. (C) The derivative ∂ ( | F ( Δ q , t ) | 2 ) / ∂ ( Δ q ) at several t, computed by linear fits to the data as shown in panel (B). All the vertical axes in this figure have arbitrary units.*

Close to the zone center ( Δ q → 0 ), where the diffuse scattering is stronger, XPCS measurements are sensitive to relaxation at short distance. If these dynamics are incoherent-like, they should have a longer relaxation time than those at higher Δ q values. This is known as de Gennes narrowing (29, 30), and has been observed in diluted glass systems (31). However, violation of de Gennes narrowing can occur in the La-cuprate family due to prevailing CDW correlations (21). In YBa2Cu3O6+y, we find that the relaxation dynamics become faster as a function of Δ q below Tc, as expected for de Gennes narrowing. However, this behavior is reversed in a broad temperature window in the normal state. In Fig. 3A, we highlight two temperatures to demonstrate these opposite trends. They are displayed even more clearly by plotting | F ( q , t ) | 2 as a function of Δ q in Fig. 3B, because | F ( q , t ) | 2 is a direct probe of speckle decorrelation strength at a given delay t. We notice the downward slope of the lighter blue line representing T = 65 K. The derivative with respect to momentum, ∂ ( | F ( q , t ) | 2 ) / ∂ ( Δ q ) , is thus negative (Fig. 3C). This negative derivative holds for most temperatures below Tc. However, over the range of temperatures greater than Tc yet below T CDW , we observe the opposite momentum dependence, where fluctuations become slower with increasing momentum transfer, as seen at T = 115 K in Fig. 3 A and B. The derivative ∂ ( | F ( q , t ) | 2 ) / ∂ ( Δ q ) is positive for these temperatures, as indicated in Fig. 3C with orange shading. Eventually, ∂ ( | F ( q , t ) | 2 ) / ∂ ( Δ q ) turns negative again above T CDW .

The speedup of lattice relaxation dynamics, which have two characteristic timescales ( τ 1 , 2 ), at Tc (Fig. 2), together with the peculiar Δ q dependence of | F ( q , t ) | 2 between Tc and T CDW violates the de Gennes narrowing description (Fig. 3) and supports the claim that this is sensitive to both CDW and superconductivity. We attempt to explain this sensitivity based on a scenario that the CDWs in YBa2Cu3O6+y are stabilized by local strains, i.e. the symmetry-breaking deviation of atoms from their ideal positions. The overall lifetime of such strained states, which scales with | F ( q , t ) | 2 , is probed by XPCS (21). Below T CDW and in the absence of superconductivity, the lifetime is longer at higher Δ q values because the CDW-driving strains are temporally stabilized. Above T CDW or below Tc, where the CDWs get suppressed by either thermal fluctuations or by competition with superconductivity, those strained states are no longer preferred, and therefore the de Gennes narrowing behavior is restored.

The two timescales in | F ( q , t ) | 2 , on the other hand, can be explained by the so-called “double-well” configuration of local atomic distortions, leading to two relaxation minima in the potential energy landscape. In YBa2Cu3O6+y, two different types of “double-well” configurations have been reported, involving either the apical (32, 33) or planar (34) oxygen ion displacements. For the latter, the planar oxygens split along the c axis into A and B sites. Such distortions are consistent with the microscopic structure of the CDW-induced atomic modulation revealed by X-ray diffraction (35). Accordingly, we can further attribute the observed atomic relaxation dynamics to the planar oxygen sites. The coupling between atomic relaxation and superconductivity is mediated via the CDW-induced “double-well” displacements of the planar oxygen atoms.

How does one interpret the anomaly at Tc? We propose that a minimal model must account for thermal fluctuations of the lattice, with an interaction due to superconducting fluctuations that turns on at Tc. To describe this effect, we introduce an interaction W between the lattice and superconducting order parameters ( ψ L / ψ SC ) within the Ginzburg–Landau phenomenological framework,

$$ [2] F = α L | ψ L | 2 + β L | ψ L | 4 + α SC | ψ SC | 2 + β SC | ψ SC | 4 + W | ψ L | 2 | ψ SC | 2 , $$

where the expansion is up to the quartic order, with α L , SC and β L , SC as expansion coefficients for their respective order parameters. In the presence of interactions, the lattice time constant can be written as (see SI Appendix for full details):

$$ [3] τ L ′ − 1 = τ L − 1 ( − α L − W | ψ SC | 2 ) . $$

In this equation, τ L is the lattice fluctuation time constant in the absence of superconducting interactions. We express τ L in a functional form used in prior XPCS studies (26):

$$ [4] τ L − 1 = τ therm − 1 exp ( − Δ E / k B T ) + τ 0 − 1 , $$

where the exponential Arrhenius term describes the thermal fluctuations with activation energy Δ E and mean relaxation time τ therm . The second term is temperature independent and may arise from quantum tunneling (26).

As shown in SI Appendix, τ L ′ captures the salient features of our experimental observations: fast dynamics at high temperatures which slow down upon cooling, a subsequent dip near Tc, and weak temperature dependence far below Tc. The model described by Eqs. 2–4 relies on the existence of a coupling between superconductivity and lattice. Lattice anomalies around Tc have been well established in YBa2Cu3O6+y (32, 36–38). On the other hand, CDWs, which inherently result in certain types of atomic displacements (35), compete with superconductivity and get partially suppressed below Tc (15). As revealed above and in ref. 21, XPCS analysis on the diffuse scattering region of cuprate superconductors probes the lattice fluctuations related to the CDWs. Considering both of these mechanisms—interactions between lattice and CDWs and those between CDWs and superconductivity—we can interpret the coupling W in our minimal model (Eq. 1) as an interaction mediated by CDWs. The presence of two different coupling parameters connecting three degrees of freedom is a hallmark of intertwining in this complex material. A more complete theoretical treatment including the involvement of the CDWs is needed to fully understand the intertwined behavior of this system.

The lattice fluctuations revealed in this study are on the order of 103 s and therefore quasi-static. While this timescale is compatible with those reported for the spontaneous CDW fluctuations in cuprates (8, 39), it is orders of magnitude slower than the CDW dynamics probed by sound velocity (40), NMR (11), ultrafast pump–probe spectroscopy (41, 42), resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (43), and inelastic X-ray scattering (44, 45). This is because the fluctuations in this study are relaxational, induced by local strains (46)—a ubiquitous property of cuprate superconductors due to carrier doping. It is well known that atomic relaxation can be slow (31, 47). Our results therefore connect the slow relaxational atomic fluctuations to the high-Tc superconductivity in cuprates.

The lattice fluctuation dynamics uncovered here tell a rich story, adding to our understanding of the complex relationship between the lattice and electronic degrees of freedom in the cuprate superconductors. These observations are made possible by XPCS, which can detect lattice instabilities on the timescale of seconds to hours, highlighting coherent X-rays as a powerful tool for the study of high-Tc superconductors, and of correlated electron systems more broadly.

## Materials and Methods

We measured one bulk, detwinned sample of YBa2Cu3O6+y with hole doping P = 0.116 in the ortho-VIII structure. This sample was measured with a Quantum Design MPMS3 Superconducting Quantum Interference Device magnetometer to have Tc = 66.4 K (SI Appendix). Two XPCS experiments were conducted at the coherent hard X-ray beamline 11-ID at the National Synchrotron Light Source II in Brookhaven National Laboratory. A 3 × 3 μm2 focused beam of 12.8 keV X-rays was diffracted from the sample in a vertical ( θ − 2 θ ) scattering geometry to an Eiger 1M area detector located 1.5 m away. After stabilizing at each temperature and aligning with a rocking curve, the diffuse scattering near the (0, 0, 5) Bragg reflection was measured at 1 Hz for 5,400 s (1.5 h). Reported uncertainties represent one SD of the data and fits.
